questions.stem: Mai leaves her salaried job at a florist to open her own flower shop in Geelong so she can choose her own hours and the products she sells. Which reason for establishing a business does this best show?
options: Gaining limited liability for the shop's debts
Being guaranteed a profit in her first year
Avoiding any need for start-up finance
Independence and control over her own work
questions.explanation: Choosing her own hours and products is about independence and control, a common non-financial reason for going into business. As a sole proprietor she has unlimited liability, and no business is guaranteed a profit.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-financial reason for establishing a business?
options: Building an asset that can be sold in the future
Seeking a higher return than a term deposit pays
The satisfaction of making a hobby a career
Expecting to earn more than an employee's wage
questions.explanation: Personal satisfaction is a non-financial reason. Earning more than a wage, building a saleable asset and beating a term deposit are all about money, so they are financial reasons.

questions.stem: Which is an example of internally sourced finance for a sole proprietor?
options: A five-year bank loan secured over the premises
An overdraft facility on the business bank account
Buying inventory from a supplier on 30-day credit
The owner contributing personal savings as capital
questions.explanation: Internal finance comes from the owner, such as a capital contribution of savings or profits kept in the business. Loans, overdrafts and supplier credit all come from outside parties, so they are externally sourced finance.

questions.stem: Jack finances new equipment for his gym with a four-year bank loan instead of his own savings. Compared with using savings, the loan will:
options: add interest expense and increase the business's liabilities
increase owner's equity by the amount that has been borrowed
reduce liabilities, because the bank pays for the equipment
leave the Balance Sheet unchanged until the loan is repaid
questions.explanation: A loan creates a liability and the interest on it is an expense that reduces profit. Borrowed money is not owner's equity, because it must be repaid to the bank.

questions.stem: Which is the main disadvantage of financing a business mainly through external borrowing?
options: Borrowing increases owner's equity and so dilutes the ownership
Interest is owed whether or not the business makes a profit
Lenders gain voting rights over the owner's business decisions
Borrowed funds cannot legally be used to buy non-current assets
questions.explanation: Interest and repayments are owed regardless of how the business performs, which adds risk and strains cash flow. A bank lender does not gain voting rights, and a loan is a liability, not owner's equity.

questions.stem: Coastal Cuts, a new hair salon, has total assets of $80,000, funded by $20,000 of the owner's capital and a $60,000 bank loan. What is its debt ratio, and what does it suggest?
options: 25%, so most of its assets are funded by the owner
33%, so its liabilities are a third of owner's equity
300%, so it owes three times what its assets are worth
75%, so the business relies heavily on external finance
questions.explanation: Debt ratio is total liabilities ÷ total assets × 100 = 60,000 ÷ 80,000 × 100 = 75%. Three-quarters of the assets are financed by borrowing, which is a high level of risk. Using capital instead of liabilities gives 25%, and dividing liabilities by equity gives 300%, which is not the debt ratio.

questions.stem: Which of the following can contribute to the failure of a small business?
options: Seeking advice from a qualified accountant before expanding
Poor cash flow management, leaving too little to pay debts
Keeping accurate and up-to-date accounting records each week
Regularly comparing actual results with the business's budget
questions.explanation: Running out of cash to pay suppliers, staff and lenders is a common cause of failure, even for a profitable business. Accurate records, budget comparisons and professional advice all help a business succeed.

questions.stem: A gift shop opens in a quiet side street with little passing foot traffic and struggles to attract customers, despite good products and fair prices. Which factor best explains its poor results?
options: A poor choice of location
A lack of internally sourced finance
The owner's unlimited liability
Recording sales on an accrual basis
questions.explanation: With good products and fair prices, the lack of customers points to the location. Unlimited liability and the accrual basis affect risk and recording, not how many customers walk in.

questions.stem: Over three years, Ridge Electrical reported a net profit each year, yet it closed because it could not pay its suppliers. Which statement best explains this?
options: Its expenses must have exceeded its revenue in each of the three years
Net profit always equals the cash a business holds at the end of the year
A business that earns a net profit cannot have any liabilities falling due
Profit is not cash; its profit may have been tied up in receivables and assets
questions.explanation: Profit is revenue earned less expenses incurred, while cash depends on when money is actually received and paid. A profitable business can still run short of cash if customers pay slowly or cash is spent on assets or loan repayments. Expenses exceeding revenue would have produced losses, not profits.

questions.stem: Which professional would a business owner usually engage to prepare the business's financial reports and tax return?
options: A marketing consultant
A solicitor
An accountant
A real estate agent
questions.explanation: Accountants prepare and interpret financial reports and tax returns. A solicitor gives legal advice, and a marketing consultant advises on promotion, not financial reporting.

questions.stem: What is the main role of a professional organisation such as CPA Australia?
options: Setting standards of conduct and training for its members
Lending start-up finance to new small businesses across Australia
Collecting GST from businesses on behalf of the federal government
Auditing the records of every small business at the end of the year
questions.explanation: Professional accounting bodies set ethical and professional standards for their members and support their ongoing training. GST is collected by the Australian Taxation Office, and the body does not lend money or audit every business.

questions.stem: An accountant mentions a client's financial difficulties to a friend at a party. Which requirement of an accountant has been breached?
options: Confidentiality
Impartiality
Comparability
Timeliness
questions.explanation: Accountants must keep their clients' information confidential, and discussing a client's affairs socially breaches this. Comparability and timeliness are qualitative characteristics of financial information, not duties of the accountant.

questions.stem: An accountant advises a client to buy a delivery van from a dealership owned by the accountant's brother, without mentioning the relationship. Which requirement is most clearly breached?
options: Timeliness, because the advice was given too late to help
Understandability, because the advice was hard to follow
Impartiality, due to an undisclosed conflict of interest
Confidentiality, because the client's details were shared
questions.explanation: Advice that could benefit the accountant's own family, given without disclosure, is not impartial. No client information was shared with anyone, so confidentiality was not breached.

questions.stem: Compared with investing $100,000 in a new business, placing it in a bank term deposit generally offers:
options: a higher expected return with higher risk
unlimited liability for the investor's debts
control over a business's daily decisions
a lower expected return but much lower risk
questions.explanation: A term deposit pays a fixed, modest return with little risk of losing the money. A business may earn more, but its return is uncertain and the owner's capital is at risk.

questions.stem: Kate's bookshop earned a net profit of $12,000 for the year, and her capital averaged $150,000. A term deposit was offering 5% a year. What is her return on owner's investment, and what does it suggest?
options: 12.5%, so the bookshop far outperforms the deposit
1.25%, which is well below the term deposit rate
8%, which beats the term deposit but carries more risk
8%, so the term deposit gives her a better return
questions.explanation: Return on owner's investment = net profit ÷ average capital × 100 = 12,000 ÷ 150,000 × 100 = 8%. That is higher than 5%, but the bookshop's return is uncertain while the deposit's is not. Dividing capital by profit gives 12.5, which is not the indicator.

questions.stem: Tom works full-time in his own business, which earns a net profit of $60,000. He could instead earn a $70,000 salary as an employee and 4% a year on his $200,000 capital in a term deposit. In total, how much annual income from these two alternatives does he forgo by running the business?
questions.explanation: The alternatives are the salary of $70,000 plus interest of 4% × $200,000 = $8,000, a total of $78,000 forgone. Comparing this with the $60,000 profit shows the business earns $18,000 less than the alternatives, but $18,000 is the shortfall, not the total income from the alternatives.

questions.stem: Which ownership structure has a single owner who has unlimited liability for the business's debts?
options: Partnership
Private company
Public company
Sole proprietor
questions.explanation: A sole proprietor owns the business alone and is personally liable for all its debts. A partnership has two or more owners, and company shareholders have limited liability.

questions.stem: Which is a feature of a private company (Pty Ltd)?
options: Its owner has unlimited personal liability for debts
It must list its shares on the Australian stock exchange
Its shareholders have limited liability for its debts
It can offer its shares for sale to the general public
questions.explanation: A private company is a separate legal entity, so its shareholders can lose only what they invested. It cannot offer shares to the public; only a public company can do that and list on a stock exchange.

questions.stem: Lena runs her café as a sole proprietor and fears losing her house if the business fails. Which change of ownership structure would protect her personal assets from the café's debts?
options: Admitting a partner to share the café's debts
Registering the café under a new business name
Forming a partnership with her brother
Forming a private company with limited liability
questions.explanation: A company is legally separate from its owners, so shareholders' personal assets are protected from the company's debts. Partners still have unlimited liability, and registering a business name does not change the legal structure.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of a public company over a private company?
options: It can raise large amounts of capital by selling shares to the public
Its owners have unlimited liability, which reassures the business's lenders
It has fewer reporting obligations than a private company has to meet
Its shares can be sold only to the existing family members who own it
questions.explanation: A public company can offer shares to the public and list on a stock exchange, giving it access to large amounts of capital. Public companies face more reporting obligations, not fewer, and their shareholders have limited liability.

questions.stem: Which statement about a sole proprietor applies the accounting entity assumption?
options: The owner's personal car loan is kept out of the business's records
The business is legally separate, so the owner has limited liability
The owner's personal assets must be included in the Balance Sheet
The owner's weekly wage from the business is recorded as an expense
questions.explanation: The entity assumption keeps the business's records separate from the owner's personal affairs, so a personal car loan is excluded. This is an accounting separation only: legally a sole proprietor and the business are the same, so liability is unlimited. Money the owner takes is Drawings, not a wage expense.

questions.stem: An asset is best defined as:
options: the residual interest in the assets of the entity after deducting all its liabilities
an increase in assets that results in an increase in owner's equity for the period
a present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events
a present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource from past events
questions.explanation: An asset is a present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events. A present obligation is a liability, the residual interest is owner's equity, and an increase in assets that raises equity describes revenue.

questions.stem: Owner's equity is best described as:
options: the residual interest in the assets after deducting liabilities
the total cash the owner has put into the business since it began
the net profit earned by the business during the reporting period
the amount the business owes to its lenders at the reporting date
questions.explanation: Owner's equity is what remains of the assets after the liabilities are deducted, so it includes capital contributed plus profits less drawings. It is not only cash contributed, and amounts owed to lenders are liabilities.

questions.stem: Which item is an expense of a service business?
options: Purchase of a new computer
Wages paid to an employee
Cash drawings by the owner
Repayment of a bank loan
questions.explanation: Wages are consumed in earning revenue, so they decrease owner's equity as an expense. Drawings are distributions to the owner, a loan repayment reduces a liability, and a computer is a non-current asset.

questions.stem: Which transaction creates revenue for Wattle Dog Grooming?
options: The owner contributing $5,000 cash
Receiving a $10,000 bank loan
Collecting cash owed by a customer
Grooming a customer's dog on credit
questions.explanation: Revenue increases owner's equity through the business's ordinary activities, and grooming on credit is earned even though cash comes later. An owner's contribution is excluded from revenue by definition, a loan is a liability, and collecting a debt only swaps one asset for another.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an asset of a hairdressing business?
options: The capital the owner contributed when the salon opened
Wages earned by staff but not yet paid at the period end
Amounts owed by customers for services already provided
Amounts owed to the supplier of the salon's hair products
questions.explanation: Amounts owed by customers are accounts receivable, a resource that will bring in cash. Amounts owed to suppliers and unpaid wages are liabilities, and the owner's capital is owner's equity.

questions.stem: A current liability is an obligation that is reasonably expected to be settled:
options: within 12 months after the end of the reporting period
more than 12 months after the end of the reporting period
within 30 days of the date of the original transaction
by the end of the useful life of the asset it financed
questions.explanation: The study design defines current liabilities as those expected to be settled within 12 months after the end of the reporting period. Anything due later is non-current.

questions.stem: Bayside Plumbing has the following items. Which is a non-current asset?
options: A van to be used for the next five years
Cash held in the business bank account
Accounts receivable due within 30 days
Plumbing supplies to be used next month
questions.explanation: A van used over several years and not held for resale is a non-current asset. Cash, short-term receivables and supplies to be used within 12 months are current assets.

questions.stem: A business has a $50,000 bank loan, of which $10,000 must be repaid in the next 12 months. How is the loan reported in the Balance Sheet?
options: $40,000 current liability and $10,000 non-current liability
$50,000 non-current liability, as the loan runs over years
$50,000 current liability, as repayments have already begun
$10,000 current liability and $40,000 non-current liability
questions.explanation: The part due within 12 months is a current liability and the rest is non-current, so the loan is split $10,000 and $40,000. Reporting it all as non-current would understate the obligations the business must meet in the coming year.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a current liability?
options: A mortgage repayable over twenty years
Accounts receivable owed by customers
Office equipment bought last month
A bank overdraft on the business's account
questions.explanation: An overdraft can be called in by the bank at any time, so it is a current liability. The mortgage is mostly non-current, accounts receivable is a current asset, and equipment is a non-current asset.

questions.stem: Recommended retail price (RRP) is a price that is:
options: set by the government for essential goods and services
suggested by the manufacturer or supplier
calculated by adding a percentage of cost to the cost price
the price at which total revenue equals total costs
questions.explanation: An RRP is the selling price suggested by the manufacturer or supplier. Adding a percentage of cost to cost describes mark-up pricing, and the point where revenue equals costs is break-even.

questions.stem: Gumnut Hardware buys a cordless drill for $80 and applies a 60% mark-up on cost. What is the selling price, before GST?
questions.explanation: The mark-up is 60% × $80 = $48, so the selling price is $80 + $48 = $128. Adding $60 treats the percentage as dollars, and $48 is only the mark-up itself.

questions.stem: A business sets its prices using a 25% mark-up on cost. What is its gross profit margin?
questions.explanation: An item costing $100 sells for $125, so gross profit is $25 and gross profit margin = 25 ÷ 125 × 100 = 20%. Mark-up is measured against cost, while gross profit margin is measured against sales, so the two percentages differ.

questions.stem: A tutor charges $60 per lesson. Variable costs are $15 per lesson and fixed costs are $9,000 a year. How many lessons must she give to break even?
options: 120 lessons
600 lessons
200 lessons
150 lessons
questions.explanation: Each lesson contributes $60 − $15 = $45 towards fixed costs, so break-even = 9,000 ÷ 45 = 200 lessons. Dividing by the $60 price ignores variable costs and gives 150.

questions.stem: A food truck sells meals for $20 each with variable costs of $8 per meal. Its fixed costs are $36,000 a year. How many meals must it sell to earn a net profit of $24,000?
options: 5,000 meals
3,000 meals
2,000 meals
7,500 meals
questions.explanation: The contribution margin is $20 − $8 = $12 per meal, so the sales needed = (36,000 + 24,000) ÷ 12 = 5,000 meals. 3,000 meals is only the break-even point, which covers fixed costs but earns no profit.

questions.stem: A business sells a product for $50 with variable costs of $30 per unit and fixed costs of $30,000. Competition forces the price down to $45. How does its break-even point change?
options: It falls from 2,000 to 1,500 units
It stays at 1,500 units, as fixed costs are unchanged
It rises from 600 to 667 units
It rises from 1,500 to 2,000 units
questions.explanation: The contribution margin falls from $20 to $15 per unit, so break-even rises from 30,000 ÷ 20 = 1,500 to 30,000 ÷ 15 = 2,000 units. Dividing fixed costs by the selling price instead of the contribution margin gives the 600 and 667 figures.

questions.stem: A drawback of setting prices only by adding a fixed mark-up to cost is that it:
options: ignores competitors' prices and what customers are willing to pay
cannot be calculated unless the business knows its fixed costs
always produces a selling price below the recommended retail price
forces the business to sell every product at its break-even point
questions.explanation: A mark-up looks only at the business's own cost, so the price may be higher than competitors' or lower than customers would happily pay. Mark-up needs only the cost price, not fixed costs, and it can produce prices above or below an RRP.

questions.stem: Which accounting report shows a business's assets, liabilities and owner's equity at a particular date?
options: Income Statement
Cash Flow Statement
Sales Journal
Balance Sheet
questions.explanation: The Balance Sheet reports financial position at a point in time. The Income Statement reports revenue and expenses for a period, and the Cash Flow Statement reports cash inflows and outflows for a period.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-financial indicator of business performance?
options: The number of customer complaints received each month
The net profit margin for the most recent financial year
The return on owner's investment compared with last year
The working capital ratio at the end of the reporting period
questions.explanation: Customer complaints are measured in numbers of events, not dollars, so they are non-financial information. Net profit margin, return on owner's investment and the working capital ratio are all calculated from financial reports.

questions.stem: A business's net profit rose from $40,000 to $48,000, while its net sales rose from $200,000 to $320,000. What happened to its net profit margin?
options: It rose from 20% to 25%
It rose from 15% to 20%
It stayed steady at 20%
It fell from 20% to 15%
questions.explanation: Net profit margin = net profit ÷ net sales × 100, which was 40,000 ÷ 200,000 = 20% and is now 48,000 ÷ 320,000 = 15%. Profit rose in dollars, but each dollar of sales now earns less profit.

questions.stem: Hilltop Bakery has current assets of $30,000 and current liabilities of $40,000. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: It has a working capital surplus of $10,000 to draw on
Its current assets more than cover its current liabilities
It may struggle to pay its short-term debts as they fall due
Its working capital ratio of 1.33:1 is a healthy position
questions.explanation: The working capital ratio is 30,000 ÷ 40,000 = 0.75:1, so current assets are not enough to meet current liabilities. The 1.33:1 figure comes from dividing the wrong way, and there is a $10,000 shortfall, not a surplus.

questions.stem: A café owner switches to compostable takeaway cups that cost 10 cents more each than plastic cups, without raising prices. What is the likely financial effect in the reports?
options: Higher expenses and a lower net profit
Higher revenue as soon as the cups are bought
Lower expenses, as the cups are compostable
A rise in owner's equity from the green choice
questions.explanation: Paying more for supplies raises expenses, and with prices unchanged, net profit falls. An environmental choice can have a real financial cost, which the owner weighs against benefits such as customer goodwill.

questions.stem: Which is a social ethical consideration for a business owner?
options: Choosing the cheapest supplier to maximise net profit
Paying staff fairly and providing safe working conditions
Reducing the packaging waste the business sends to landfill
Installing solar panels to cut the business's emissions
questions.explanation: Fair pay and safe conditions concern people, so they are social considerations. Cutting waste and emissions are environmental considerations, and choosing the cheapest supplier is a financial one.

questions.stem: Before buying a business, Ella is shown an Income Statement from which the seller has left out several large expenses. Which qualitative characteristic does this breach?
options: Understandability
Faithful representation
Timeliness
Comparability
questions.explanation: A faithful representation must be complete, free from material error and neutral, and leaving out expenses makes the report incomplete and biased towards a higher profit. The report may be clear and on time, so understandability and timeliness are not the problem.
